what_its_for: Meperidine is a strong pain medicine (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain, such as pain after surgery or during certain medical procedures. It works in your brain and nervous system to change how your body feels and responds to pain.
how_to_take: Take meperidine exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a tablet or liquid that you swallow by mouth. You can take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablets — swallow them whole. Use the measuring device that came with your liquid medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon, as it may give you the wrong amount. Never take more than prescribed, and never take it more often than your doctor said.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your pain level, weight, age, and other health conditions. For adults, the usual dose is 50 to 150 mg every 3 to 4 hours as needed for pain. Do not change your dose on your own. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions. This medicine is usually used for only a short period of time because of the risk of side effects with longer use.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and you are taking meperidine on a scheduled basis, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are taking it only when needed for pain (as-needed basis), just take it when you have pain and follow your doctor's instructions.
storage: Store meperidine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in a safe, secure place — away from children and anyone else who should not have access to it. Never share your medicine with anyone else; this is illegal and can cause serious harm or death. If you have leftover medicine, ask your pharmacist about a safe take-back program or a medicine drop-off location in your community. Do not flush it down the toilet unless the label or your pharmacist tells you to.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking meperidine — it can cause dangerous or even life-threatening side effects like extreme drowsiness, slowed breathing, or death. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Do not take other medicines that make you sleepy (such as sleep aids, muscle relaxers, anti-anxiety medicines, or other pain medicines) without asking your doctor first. Avoid taking meperidine if you have used an MAO inhibitor (such as phenelzine, selegiline, or tranylcypromine) in the past 14 days — this combination can cause a very serious and potentially fatal reaction.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme drowsiness or you cannot be awakened; severe dizziness or confusion; seizures; fast or irregular heartbeat; muscle twitching or shaking; severe agitation or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there); signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if your pain is not well controlled, or if you feel you need more medicine than prescribed.
when_it_works: Meperidine usually starts to relieve pain within 10 to 15 minutes when given by injection, or within 30 to 60 minutes when taken by mouth. The pain-relieving effect typically lasts 2 to 4 hours. Take it as soon as your pain starts — do not wait until the pain becomes very bad, as it works better when taken early.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Meperidine is generally NOT recommended for older adults because a byproduct of the drug called normeperidine can build up in the body and cause serious side effects like seizures and confusion. Talk to your doctor about safer pain medicine options. Children: Meperidine should only be used in children if specifically prescribed by a doctor, at a carefully calculated dose based on body weight. Pregnant women: Do not use meperidine during labor and delivery or during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary, as it can cause breathing problems in the newborn baby and may cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby after birth. Breastfeeding women: Meperidine passes into breast milk and can cause serious harm to a nursing baby. Ask your doctor about safer options if you are breastfeeding. People with kidney or liver problems: Use with extreme caution; normeperidine (a harmful breakdown product) can build up and increase the risk of seizures. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or choose a different pain medicine.
